title: Does Alcohol Cause Acne? What Drinking Really Does to Your Skin
excerpt: Does drinking cause breakouts? How alcohol affects acne through sleep, stress hormones, sugar, and inflammation, why it is often rosacea instead, and what to do about it.
metaDescription: Does alcohol cause acne? How drinking worsens breakouts through sleep, sugar, and stress hormones, the rosacea link, and how to protect your skin.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** alcohol is not a direct cause of acne in the way that clogged pores, oil, bacteria, and hormones are. There's no good evidence that a few drinks on their own will create pimples on clear skin. But drinking can make existing acne worse through a handful of indirect routes: worse sleep, a stress-hormone bump, sugary mixers, late-night food, inflammation, and skipping your skincare routine when you get home. It's also a well-known trigger for rosacea, a different skin condition that produces red bumps people often mistake for acne. So if your skin looks worse after a weekend out, you're probably not imagining it. You're just seeing several small effects stack up rather than one big one.

**The quick rules:** If you're acne-prone, drink less on nights you care about your skin, choose lower-sugar drinks, alternate with water, wash your face before bed no matter how late it is, and protect your sleep. If you take a prescription acne medicine, especially isotretinoin (Accutane and its generics), ask your dermatologist or pharmacist about alcohol before you drink. And if what you're seeing is redness, flushing, and small red bumps across your cheeks and nose rather than blackheads and whiteheads, think rosacea, not acne.

> **When to see a doctor or dermatologist.** This article is general information, not medical advice. **Book an appointment if** you have painful, deep, or cyst-like lumps; acne that is leaving dark marks or scars; breakouts that haven't improved after two to three months of consistent over-the-counter treatment; persistent facial redness, visible small blood vessels, or gritty, irritated eyes (possible rosacea); or sudden adult acne along with irregular periods or new facial or body hair (worth checking for hormonal causes such as PCOS). **Get urgent care** if you get hives, lip or tongue swelling, or trouble breathing after drinking, which can be an allergic reaction, or if you notice yellow skin or eyes, which points to the liver rather than the skin. Call 911 in an emergency.

## How Acne Actually Forms (and Why That Matters for Alcohol)

To judge whether alcohol causes acne, it helps to know what acne is. Dermatologists describe four main ingredients:

1. **Too much oil (sebum).** The oil glands in your skin, which sit at the base of hair follicles, make sebum. Hormones called androgens turn production up.
2. **Clogged pores.** Skin cells that line the follicle don't shed properly, stick together, and plug the opening. That plug is a comedone: a blackhead if it's open, a whitehead if it's closed.
3. **Bacteria.** A normal skin bacterium called *Cutibacterium acnes* (formerly *Propionibacterium acnes*) thrives in the oily, low-oxygen plug.
4. **Inflammation.** Your immune system reacts, and the plug turns into a red, sore pimple, a pustule, or a deeper nodule.

Here's the important part for anyone blaming last night's drinks: **a pimple doesn't form overnight.** The tiny plug at the start of a breakout, called a microcomedone, develops over a period of weeks before you can see it. What a night out *can* do is push an already-forming plug into an inflamed, visible spot sooner, or make the inflammation around it angrier. That's why a "beer breakout" two days later is usually a flare of something that was already on its way, not a pimple alcohol built from scratch.

None of the four drivers above has ethanol as a main ingredient. Alcohol can nudge several of them, though, and that's where the real story is.

## The Indirect Ways Drinking Can Make Breakouts Worse

There isn't a big, clean study that gave people alcohol and counted their pimples. Most of what we know comes from understanding what alcohol does to the body and what's known to influence acne. Put those together and you get a set of plausible links. None of them is dramatic alone. Together they explain why many people notice worse skin after heavy weekends.

### 1. It wrecks your sleep

Alcohol helps you fall asleep, then fragments the second half of the night and cuts into REM sleep. Short or broken sleep raises stress hormones and is linked to more inflammation in general. Many dermatologists list poor sleep as a common acne aggravator, and most people with acne have noticed their skin is worse during stretches of bad sleep. If you want the details on why you wake at 4 a.m. after drinking, see our guide on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking).

### 2. It nudges stress hormones up

Drinking, and especially the hangover that follows, raises cortisol, the body's main stress hormone. Stress is a well-recognized acne trigger. Studies of students during exam periods have found that acne tends to get worse as stress rises. Alcohol isn't the same thing as exam stress, but it pushes the body in a similar direction, and a rough hangover morning plus a short night stacks the effect.

### 3. It can shift hormones

Acne is heavily driven by androgens, the hormones that tell oil glands to make more sebum. Research on alcohol and sex hormones is mixed and depends on sex, dose, and pattern of drinking. Some studies have found that drinking can raise estrogen levels and, in some women, androgen levels too. In men, regular heavy drinking tends to lower testosterone over time. The net effect on oil production for any one person is hard to predict, and there's no good evidence that moderate drinking reliably changes acne through hormones. It's a reason heavy, regular drinking may matter more than an occasional glass.

### 4. Sugary drinks and late-night food

This is one of the better-supported links, and it isn't really about the alcohol. Diets high in fast-digesting carbohydrates (a high glycemic load) have been linked to worse acne, and a randomized trial in young Australian men found that a low-glycemic diet improved acne compared with a typical diet. Many cocktails, sweet wines, hard seltzers with added sugar, alcopops, and soda mixers deliver a lot of quick sugar. Add a 1 a.m. pizza or fries, and the evening's glycemic load is high. Cream liqueurs and milky cocktails add dairy, and observational studies have linked milk intake (particularly skim milk) to acne, although that evidence is weaker and doesn't apply to everyone.

### 5. Inflammation and your immune system

Heavy drinking increases inflammation across the body and changes how the immune system works. Acne is an inflammatory condition, so it makes sense that a body under extra inflammatory load might have angrier breakouts. Our [guide to alcohol and inflammation](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-inflammation-complete-health-impact-guide-2025) covers this in more depth. This link is reasonable but mostly indirect; it has not been measured well in acne specifically.

### 6. Dehydration (smaller than people think)

Alcohol makes you pee more by suppressing a hormone that tells your kidneys to hold onto water. Dehydrated skin can look dull and feel tight, and fine lines show more. But there's no good evidence that dehydration causes acne. Drinking extra water is good for how you feel and how your skin looks, yet it won't clear breakouts on its own. Treat the "alcohol dries you out so you break out" story with some skepticism.

### 7. The behavior around drinking

Some of the most practical causes are the least scientific:

- **Sleeping in your makeup** or sunscreen after a late night.
- **Touching your face** more when you're relaxed and in a crowd.
- **Sweat and heat** in packed bars or on dance floors, followed by not washing.
- **Skipping your routine.** If your acne treatment works only when you use it nightly, missing two or three nights a week adds up.
- **Smoking or vaping** more when drinking, which isn't good for skin either.

For a lot of people, simply washing their face before bed after a night out does more for their skin than any change to what they drink.

## Is It Acne, or Is It Rosacea?

This is the section most articles skip, and it might be the most useful one. Rosacea is a common, long-term skin condition that causes facial redness, flushing, visible small blood vessels, and often small red bumps and pus-filled spots. It used to be called "acne rosacea," and the bumps look enough like acne that people often treat it as acne. But it's a different condition with different triggers and treatments.

Alcohol is one of the best-known rosacea triggers. Surveys by the National Rosacea Society have consistently listed alcohol, particularly red wine, among the most commonly reported flare triggers. A large study of women in the Nurses' Health Study II, published in the *Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology* in 2017, found that higher alcohol intake was associated with a higher risk of developing rosacea, with white wine and liquor showing the clearest links.

Signs it may be rosacea rather than acne:

- You flush easily, and the redness lingers.
- The bumps sit mostly on the central face: cheeks, nose, chin, forehead.
- There are **no blackheads or whiteheads**. Acne has comedones; rosacea doesn't.
- Your skin stings or burns with many products.
- Your eyes often feel gritty, dry, or irritated.
- You're over 30, with fair skin, and the problem started later in life (though anyone can get it).

Rosacea doesn't respond well to some classic acne treatments, and harsh acne products can make it worse. If this list sounds familiar, it's worth seeing a dermatologist. And if your main issue is turning red when you drink, rather than bumps, our guides on [red face after drinking](/never-hungover/red-face-after-drinking) and the [Asian flush](/never-hungover/complete-guide-asian-flush-comprehensive) explain the flushing side, which is a separate issue from both acne and rosacea.

## Beer, Wine, Liquor: Does the Type of Drink Matter?

People often ask whether one kind of drink is worse for skin. There's very little research comparing drink types for acne specifically, so here's what can reasonably be said.

### Does beer cause acne?

Beer is often blamed, usually because of its carbohydrates, yeast, or gluten. There's no good evidence that beer causes acne more than other drinks at the same alcohol dose. Its carb load is moderate and depends on the style, and the gluten connection only matters for people with celiac disease, where a separate skin rash (dermatitis herpetiformis) can occur. If you drink several pints, the volume of carbs plus the late-night food that tends to come with beer is the more likely culprit.

### Does wine cause acne?

Wine, especially red wine, is a strong flushing and rosacea trigger for many people. If your "wine breakouts" come with redness and warmth, rosacea or flushing is the first thing to consider. Sweet and dessert wines also carry more sugar. Dry wines have less.

### Does liquor cause acne?

Spirits are almost sugar-free on their own. The issue is what goes in the glass with them. Vodka with soda water and lime is a very different drink from a margarita made with sweet mix or a rum and cola. If you're trying to limit sugar, choose spirits with soda water, or with a splash of juice rather than a full glass of it.

### Hard seltzers and "clean" drinks

Some hard seltzers are low in sugar, and some aren't. Check the label. Calling a drink "clean" doesn't change its alcohol content, which is what drives the sleep, cortisol, and inflammation effects described above.

**The practical takeaway:** the amount you drink and what you mix it with matter more than whether it's beer, wine, or spirits.

## Alcohol and Acne Medications: What to Ask Your Doctor

If you're treating acne with prescription medicine, this is the part to take seriously. The information below is general. Your prescriber or pharmacist knows your doses and health history, so **talk to your doctor or pharmacist before drinking on any of these medicines.**

### Isotretinoin (Accutane, Absorica, Claravis, and generics)

Isotretinoin is processed by the liver and can raise liver enzymes and blood fats called triglycerides. Alcohol can do both too. That's why prescribers commonly advise avoiding or strictly limiting alcohol during treatment, and why your blood is checked during the course. Isotretinoin also causes very dry skin and lips, which drinking won't help. Ask your dermatologist what's acceptable for you, and don't assume a "normal" amount is fine.

### Oral antibiotics (doxycycline, minocycline)

These are often prescribed for moderate inflammatory acne. Moderate drinking is not considered a major interaction for most people. In people who drink heavily on a regular basis, alcohol can speed up how fast the body clears doxycycline, which may make it less effective. Alcohol can also add to stomach upset. Ask your pharmacist about your specific prescription. Our guide to [doxycycline and alcohol](/never-hungover/doxycycline-and-alcohol) covers this question in more detail.

### Spironolactone

Spironolactone is often used for hormonal acne in women. It lowers blood pressure and can cause dizziness, and alcohol can add to that light-headed feeling, especially when you stand up quickly. Drink water, take it easy, and check with your doctor.

### Topical treatments

Benzoyl peroxide, adapalene, tretinoin, salicylic acid, and azelaic acid don't interact with drinking in any meaningful way. The risk is just forgetting to apply them after a late night. Keep them by the sink so they're part of brushing your teeth.

## "Alcohol in Skincare" Is a Different Question

People sometimes mix up drinking alcohol with alcohol in skincare products. They are different things. Some toners and acne products contain ethanol or "alcohol denat." because it helps products dry fast and feel light. In high amounts it can dry and irritate skin, which some people with acne or rosacea find aggravating. "Fatty alcohols" such as cetyl or stearyl alcohol are a different family entirely; they're waxy, moisturizing ingredients and don't dry the skin.

Also, drinking alcohol doesn't "disinfect" your skin from the inside or kill acne bacteria. That idea comes up online now and then, and there's nothing to it.

## Why Some People Notice It More Than Others

If your friend drinks the same amount and has clear skin, you're not imagining the difference. Acne-prone skin is largely genetic and hormonal. People whose skin is already on the edge, with lots of tiny clogged pores ready to flare, will notice small pushes like poor sleep and sugar more. Teenagers and people in their twenties with active acne, women whose acne tracks their cycle, and anyone with rosacea tend to be most sensitive. People with clear, non-acne-prone skin may see no change at all.

Your menstrual cycle can also confuse the picture. Many women break out in the week before their period. If that's also when you happened to go out, alcohol can look guilty when the cycle is doing most of the work. Tracking both for a couple of months can help you sort it out.

## How to Tell If Alcohol Is Behind Your Breakouts

Because acne takes weeks to form and has many triggers, one bad morning doesn't prove much. A simple personal test works better:

1. **Keep a short log for six to eight weeks.** Note drinks per week, what you drank, sleep, your cycle if relevant, and how your skin looks once a week. Photos in the same light help.
2. **Then cut back for four to six weeks.** Have fewer drinks, or switch to lower-sugar options, while keeping your skincare routine the same.
3. **Compare.** If your skin is clearly better during the lighter weeks, alcohol (or what comes with it) is likely part of your picture. If nothing changes, look elsewhere: your products, your treatment, hormones, or stress.

Changing only one thing at a time is the key. If you change your drinking, your cleanser, and your diet in the same week, you won't know what helped.

## How to Drink Without Wrecking Your Skin

You don't have to give up drinking to look after acne-prone skin. These habits address the indirect links above:

- **Set a limit before you go out.** Fewer drinks means less sleep disruption, less cortisol, and less inflammation.
- **Pick lower-sugar drinks.** Dry wine, light beer, or spirits with soda water instead of sugary cocktails, sweet mixers, and cream liqueurs.
- **Alternate with water.** One glass of water per drink slows your pace and helps you feel better the next day.
- **Eat a real meal before drinking**, ideally with protein, fiber, and some fat, so you're less likely to end the night with fast food.
- **Wash your face before bed, every time.** A gentle cleanser takes a minute. Keep micellar water or cleansing wipes by the bed for nights you're tired, though a proper wash is better.
- **Don't skip your treatment.** Apply your benzoyl peroxide, adapalene, or prescription cream as usual.
- **Change your pillowcase** often. It's a small thing, but helps if you sleep on the same side every night.
- **Protect your sleep.** Stop drinking a couple of hours before bed when you can, and give yourself a lie-in after a late night if possible.
- **Don't pick or squeeze** the next morning. It makes marks and scars more likely.
- **If you have rosacea**, notice which drinks flare you and avoid those. Many people find red wine is the worst offender.

If your face looks puffy rather than broken out the morning after, that's usually fluid shifting rather than acne; our guide to [alcohol face bloating](/never-hungover/alcohol-face-bloating) explains what's going on and how fast it fades.

## What Works for Acne Regardless of Drinking

Cutting back on alcohol may help, but it rarely clears moderate acne alone. Proven treatments make a much bigger difference:

- **Benzoyl peroxide** (2.5% to 5% is often as effective as stronger versions and less irritating) reduces acne bacteria.
- **Adapalene** gel 0.1% (Differin), a retinoid that keeps pores from clogging, has been sold over the counter in the US since 2016.
- **Salicylic acid** helps unclog pores, especially for blackheads and whiteheads.
- **Azelaic acid** helps both acne and the redness of rosacea.
- **Non-comedogenic** moisturizer and sunscreen, so you aren't clogging pores with your other products.

Give any new routine eight to twelve weeks before judging it, because acne takes that long to turn over. If over-the-counter treatment isn't working after that, or if you have painful nodules or scarring, see a dermatologist. Prescription options are far more effective for moderate to severe acne.

## The Bigger Picture: Alcohol and Your Skin Over Time

Acne is only one part of how alcohol affects skin. Over years, regular heavy drinking is linked to flushing that becomes permanent, more visible blood vessels, a duller complexion, and faster signs of aging. Our deeper look at [alcohol and skin health](/never-hungover/alcohol-skin-health-anti-aging-impact-analysis-2025) covers those long-term effects. For an occasional social drinker, the skin effects are mostly short-lived and reversible: better sleep, more water, and a consistent routine usually bring things back within days to weeks.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

Some people take DHM (dihydromyricetin), a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree, on nights they drink. Research on DHM suggests it may support how the body processes alcohol and may ease how you feel the next day, though most of the evidence comes from animal and lab studies with limited human data. **There is no good evidence that DHM prevents or treats acne**, and it isn't a substitute for drinking less or for acne treatment.

Where it may be relevant is indirect. If you feel less rough the morning after, you're more likely to sleep in properly, eat a decent breakfast, and stick to your routine, all of which help your skin. If you want to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains timing and amounts. If you take any prescription medicine, including acne medicine, check with your pharmacist before adding a supplement.

## The Bottom Line

Alcohol isn't a direct cause of acne, and a couple of drinks won't create breakouts on clear skin. But for people with acne-prone skin, drinking can make things worse through poor sleep, a stress-hormone bump, sugary mixers, late-night food, inflammation, and skipped skincare. It's also a well-documented trigger for rosacea, which is easy to mistake for acne. Drink less on nights that matter, choose lower-sugar drinks, wash your face before bed, protect your sleep, and use proven acne treatments. If you're on isotretinoin or another prescription acne medicine, ask your doctor about alcohol first. And if you have painful nodules, scarring, or persistent redness, see a dermatologist.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does alcohol cause acne?**

Not directly. Acne is driven by oil, clogged pores, bacteria, and inflammation, and alcohol isn't a main cause of any of them. There's no good evidence that a few drinks create pimples on clear skin. But drinking can make existing acne worse indirectly through poor sleep, higher stress hormones, sugary mixers, late-night food, inflammation, and skipping your skincare routine.

**Why do I break out after drinking?**

Usually because several small effects stack up: broken sleep, a cortisol bump from the hangover, sugary drinks or late-night food, sweat, and going to bed without washing your face. Pimples also take weeks to form, so a spot that appears a day or two after a night out was probably already developing and simply flared. If the bumps come with redness and flushing and there are no blackheads or whiteheads, it may be rosacea rather than acne.

**Does beer cause acne?**

There's no good evidence that beer causes acne more than other drinks at the same alcohol dose. Its carbohydrates, and the late-night food that often comes with several pints, may matter for some people. The gluten link only applies to people with celiac disease, who can get a separate itchy rash called dermatitis herpetiformis.

**Can wine make acne or rosacea worse?**

Wine, especially red wine, is one of the most commonly reported rosacea triggers, and a large study of women found that higher alcohol intake was associated with a higher risk of rosacea. If your 'wine breakouts' come with redness, warmth, and flushing, rosacea is worth considering. Sweet wines also add more sugar than dry ones.

**Can I drink alcohol while taking Accutane (isotretinoin)?**

Ask your dermatologist before drinking. Isotretinoin can raise liver enzymes and triglycerides, and alcohol can raise both too, so prescribers commonly advise avoiding or strictly limiting alcohol during treatment. Your blood is monitored during the course for this reason. Don't assume a normal amount is fine without checking.

**Will quitting alcohol clear my acne?**

It may help if drinking is affecting your sleep, diet, and routine, but it rarely clears moderate acne by itself. Proven treatments such as benzoyl peroxide, adapalene, salicylic acid, or prescription medicines make a much bigger difference. To test alcohol's role, cut back for four to six weeks while keeping everything else the same, and compare.

**Does drinking water after alcohol prevent breakouts?**

Water helps you feel better and can make skin look less dull, but there's no good evidence that dehydration causes acne or that extra water prevents breakouts. Alternating water with drinks is still worth doing, mostly because it slows your pace and reduces how much you drink overall.

**Does DHM help with acne from drinking?**

There's no good evidence that DHM prevents or treats acne. DHM has research on alcohol metabolism and next-day symptoms, mostly from animal and lab studies with limited human data. Any skin benefit would be indirect, from feeling well enough to sleep properly and keep your routine. It isn't a substitute for acne treatment.
